reachable: Yes, in the only sense that applies to a train-only head. aux_loss is called from exactly two places in the repo — evolve/harness.py:104 (training) and eval/guard_reach.py:220 (the gate) — and from no scoring path, so it contributes literally nothing at the scored position, as claimed. What must reach the score is a learned change to the arch's forward, and it does: on real batches with the real genome the aux is nonzero (3.34 at full ramp) and backward touches 86 of 127 net parameters. The hinge is exactly at the margin at init (l_ca = 1.0078, mean lp_native - lp_swap = -0.008), i.e. the loss behaves as the hypothesis predicts for a non-tracking predictor. One caveat on where the gradient lands: at init the only transport-machinery parameters receiving gradient are tp_out.weight/bias, because r23's readout is zero-init; addr_*/tp_*_gate/ptr_* stay at exactly zero gradient until tp_out moves off zero. That is the arch's bit-identical-at-init design, not a head defect, but the claim that the head "supplies the missing gradient ... to the move gates" is only true after tp_out has taken a step.
solves_outside_model: Clean. No command text is parsed anywhere in the head — I read the whole module and it touches only tensors; all mining is embedding-distance clustering, and I verified the clustering is effectively exact-duplicate detection (precision 0.9996, recall 1.000 against exact equality of the rendered observation strings; the mutating/content-free flag matches "empty output" on 7608 of 7612 steps), so the "0.02-of-mean-distance threshold is safe" claim holds. Nothing about which content ends where is computed in Python and handed to the model. The counterfactual is an input perturbation built from real command embeddings already in the batch, applied at train time only, and the supervision label is the observation the trajectory itself recorded at step j. wrap registers no parameters, adds no module, and does not re-point forward (net parameter count unchanged at 5,468,483; scored forward bit-identical to the arch's own). The head is on the head axis, not the stream axis, so the read-token-parity invariant does not cover it — but it does not need to, because the head never runs at scoring.
summary:
The mechanism is real, valid, reachable and honest about the eval — but two load-bearing factual claims in the hypothesis are wrong, and I verified both by execution on the real training root.

WHAT CHECKS OUT. The mining is exactly what it says: label-free, embedding-only, no command text. On real batches it fires on 100% of rows, and the mined (i, j) pairs are genuine (expose, read) pairs of a content routed by a chain of mv's — e.g. `cat /tmp/w/cups/var/log/syslog.log` at i=7 read back as `cat /tmp/w/cups/g97/f738.tmp.8` at j=22 after a 3-hop chain. Duplicate detection is effectively exact (precision 0.9996 / recall 1.000 vs rendered-text equality), vindicating the 0.02 threshold the author could not measure. tok_nat reconstructs the batch bit-exactly, only command positions differ between arms, the hinge sits at the full margin at init as predicted, and gradient reaches the net.

WHAT DOES NOT. (1) The stated baseline is wrong: the parent head is NOT a passthrough. r23 inherits transition_from_emb from r18 via r22, `_disabled` is False, and the parent aux is 0.155 at full ramp. The child therefore removes a live auxiliary and adds another; the parent-child delta means something different from what the hypothesis says. (2) The counterfactual is not "the same destinations ... only the move commands re-drawn". The scored role-swap keeps the destination sequence byte-identical (cups_probe.py:562 reuses `dsts`) and changes only sources. This head instead splices in unrelated commands: measured, the read location's path appears among the intervening commands in 60.4% of native arms but only 8.3% of counterfactual arms, and donors mention the same capability pack as the read only 6.5% of the time (vs 41.9% for the commands they replace), are `mv` only 43.2% of the time, and come from a different trajectory 35.1% of the time. So the very shortcut the author says he closed with same-row donors — "an unfamiliar command appeared, so be uncertain" — is wide open, and a model that takes it is a model whose behaviour cancels to exactly zero across the two scored arms. The hinge can be driven to zero without any chain tracking.

Nothing here makes the candidate invalid or lets it climb the score dishonestly — it may well produce a null. The problem is that it will be archived under a description asserting it trains an unbiased stand-in for comp_ca against a dead parent head, and neither half of that is true.

WHAT I COULD NOT CHECK: whether the trained net actually takes the surface shortcut rather than learning to route (needs a full GPU run and the swap probe); whether comp_ca moves at all; whether the 1.6x CPU step-time ratio holds on GPU; the `net.eval()` batch-norm assumption for archs other than this genome's (irrelevant here — r23 uses dropout only).

divergences.claim: hypothesis §1: "The parent's arch is r23_dual_address_transport_pointer, which subclasses R22PrefixContentXAttention and defines no such method, so cfg['_disabled'] ... is True and the head returns a hard 0.0 on every step of every run. The parent's head axis is, as scored, a passthrough."
divergences.what_the_code_does: r23 inherits transition_from_emb through R22PrefixContentXAttention from R18PathStateLatentTransition (defined at evolve/chunks/arch/r18_pathstate_latent_transition_worldmodel.py:239). The parent head is LIVE on this genome: _disabled is False and it returns a real, growing auxiliary loss. So the child does not add a mechanism to an empty axis — it REMOVES a live auxiliary loss and substitutes a different one, and any child-vs-parent delta confounds the two.
divergences.evidence: Executed with the candidate's own genome, head swapped to the parent's: `disabled? False`; parent aux = 2.9e-06 at step 1 (ramp), 0.1531 at step 500, 0.1553 at step 2000. `callable(getattr(net,'transition_from_emb',None))` is True on the built r23 net.

divergences.claim: hypothesis §2: the counterfactual is "the same board, the same read command, the same destinations, the same depth, only the move commands re-drawn" — "an unbiased stand-in for native_hit - swap_stayed".
divergences.what_the_code_does: Lines 195-214 replace each on-path command embedding with an independently sampled OFF-path content-free command from the same row (or another row). Destinations are NOT preserved: the substituted commands reference entirely different paths. The scored role-swap does the opposite — evolve/cups_probe.py:562 emits `f"mv {loc2[c]} {dst}"` reusing the native `dsts` list, so the destination sequence is byte-identical across the scored arms and only the sources change. The two constructions are structurally different, and the train-time one admits a surface discriminator that provably contributes exactly zero at scoring: "does the read location's path appear among the intervening commands".
divergences.evidence: Measured over 144 mined windows from 6 real training batches (data/dockerfs3-cupsF-treat-nocwd): the read command's path appears verbatim in an intervening command in 60.4% of NATIVE arms vs 8.3% of the head's COUNTERFACTUAL arms; mean path-token overlap 0.618 vs 0.259. A detector using only that cue separates the head's two arms on ~55% of mined windows without any routing, and gives identical output on both scored arms.

divergences.claim: hypothesis §2c and §4: the donor is "a real move command from a different group in the same trajectory"; "I chose SAME-ROW donors specifically to close [the shallow 'an unfamiliar command appeared, so be uncertain' detector]: the substituted command is a real move command from the same trajectory over the same style of paths, so there is no out-of-distribution cue to key on."
divergences.what_the_code_does: Because rows are selected top-k by largest j-i (line 177), the mined interval usually spans most of the row and leaves no off-path mutating step, so the cross-row fallback (line 198-201) fires far more than as an edge case. Donors are frequently not moves at all (empty-output `ls`, `cat x > y` redirects are classified content-free) and usually reference a different capability family than the read.
divergences.evidence: Measured over 1583 on-path substitutions across 8 real batches: donor is an `mv` 43.2% of the time (originals: 79.2%); donor comes from a DIFFERENT trajectory 35.1% of the time; donor mentions the same capability pack (cups vs cvar) as the read command only 6.5% of the time (originals: 41.9%), and the same group only 4.5% (originals: 17.4%). The stated defense is not in force.

divergences.claim: hypothesis §2c: "same pad pattern, same positions, same observation tokens, same non-mutating commands. The two arms differ ONLY in which moves were issued."
divergences.what_the_code_does: On-path is defined as content-free (empty-observation) steps, which in this data includes empty-output `ls` steps, not only `mv`. Those get substituted too. Everything else in the claim is exact.
divergences.evidence: Row 0 of batch 0: on-path = [mv…, `ls /usr/src`, mv…, mv…, mv…]; row 4: on-path includes `ls /lib/firmware`. Verified tok_nat reconstructs tok[rows] bit-exactly (torch.equal True) and only command positions differ between arms (mean 7.7 of 64 token positions changed).

divergences.claim: hypothesis §4: "roughly one extra full-batch forward and backward per step under the default batch size — call it about 2x step time, unmeasured".
divergences.what_the_code_does: R = min(ceil(0.5*64), 24) = 24, so the aux forward is 48 rows against a 64-row main batch. Correctly labelled unmeasured; the measured factor is somewhat below the estimate.
divergences.evidence: 6 real training steps on CPU via evolve.harness._train: baseline_passthrough 10.54s, parent r18 head 9.46s, this head 15.21s → ~1.6x the parent, not 2x. GPU ratio unverified.
